source_refs.note: Exercise 11.1, Question 2: book page 290 (Q1-Q8). The book prints no answers for Unit 11; every answer here is ours.

blocks.prompt: 2. Construct a vector function for a particle moving in a circle.
blocks.explanation:
An open construction question: we build \(\mathbf{r}(t)\) for circular motion.
We choose the circle (centre \(O\), radius \(a\)) and the speed of turning (\(\omega\) radians per second).
Plan: the book's three steps: components from the angle turned, vector form, domain; then check that \(|\mathbf{r}(t)| = a\).
steps:
Given: a particle moves on a circle.
To find: a vector function \(\mathbf{r}(t)\) for its position.
Method: the three steps of 11.1.3. Let the circle have centre \(O\) and radius \(a\); the particle starts at \((a, 0)\) at \(t = 0\) and turns anticlockwise at a constant \(\omega\) radians per second.

Step-1: Determine the components
After \(t\) seconds the radius has turned through
\[\theta = \omega t\]
\[x(t) = a\cos(\omega t)\]
\[y(t) = a\sin(\omega t)\]
Why: a point on a circle of radius \(a\) at angle \(\theta\) from the \(x\)-axis is \((a\cos\theta, a\sin\theta)\) (trigonometric ratios in a right triangle with hypotenuse \(a\)).

Step-2: Combine into vector form
\[\mathbf{r}(t) = a\cos(\omega t)\,\hat{i}\]
\[\quad + a\sin(\omega t)\,\hat{j}\]
Why: the \(x\)-component goes with \(\hat{i}\) and the \(y\)-component with \(\hat{j}\), as in 11.1.2.

Step-3: Specify the domain
\[t \ge 0\]
One full turn takes
\[T = \dfrac{2\pi}{\omega} \text{ seconds}\]
Why: \(t\) is time measured from the start. Both components are defined for every real \(t\), so time is the only restriction.

A particular case: \(a = 3\), \(\omega = 1\)
\[\mathbf{r}(t) = 3\cos t\,\hat{i} + 3\sin t\,\hat{j}\]
At \(t = 0, \frac{\pi}{2}, \pi, \frac{3\pi}{2}\) the particle is at \((3, 0), (0, 3), (-3, 0), (0, -3)\), and back at \((3, 0)\) when \(t = 2\pi\).
Why: putting values of \(t\) shows the particle going round anticlockwise (see the figure).

Check: the particle stays on the circle
\[|\mathbf{r}(t)|^2 = a^2\cos^2(\omega t)\]
\[\quad + a^2\sin^2(\omega t)\]
\[= a^2 \cdot 1 = a^2\]
\[|\mathbf{r}(t)| = a \;\checkmark\]
Why: \(\cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta = 1\). The distance from \(O\) is always \(a\), so every position is on the circle.
blocks.final_answer: \(\mathbf{r}(t) = a\cos(\omega t)\,\hat{i} + a\sin(\omega t)\,\hat{j},\ t \ge 0\) (circle of radius \(a\), centre \(O\), angular speed \(\omega\)); for example \(\mathbf{r}(t) = 3\cos t\,\hat{i} + 3\sin t\,\hat{j}\).

answer_figure.alt: Circle of radius 3 with centre at the origin. Points t = 0 at (3, 0), t = pi/2 at (0, 3), t = pi at (-3, 0) and t = 3pi/2 at (0, -3). Arrows show anticlockwise motion; a pink arrow from O is the position vector r(t) making angle t with the x-axis.
answer_figure.caption: The particle r(t) = 3cos t i + 3sin t j goes anticlockwise round the circle of radius 3 (our drawing)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: The textbook prints no answers for Exercise 11.1 (none for the whole of Unit 11). Every answer on this page is ours: worked out step by step, checked independently with a computer algebra system (sympy) and compared with a solution book. This question is open: many correct answers exist. Ours is one model answer built with the book's three steps (11.1.3); any function that models the motion correctly is also right.
